problem:
The intersection of the planes $2x-y-3z-8=0$ and $x+2y-3z-4=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$

feedback.problem:
The intersection of the planes $2x-y-6=0$ and $y+z+6=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},0,{a}_{3}⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{3},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We're given that there exists a point on the line where $y=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

$$
2x-0-6=0\,⟹\,x=3,
$$

and substituting $y=0$ into the second equation gives

$$
0+z+6=0\,⟹\,z=-6.
$$

Therefore, $a=⟨3,0,-6⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $2x-y-6=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨2,-1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $y+z+6=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} \\  & =⟨2,-1,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-2j+2k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨3,0,-6⟩+t⟨-1,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{3}=3-6=-3,$ and $b=⟨-1,-2,2⟩.$
